clue.text: Pub's daily hours in this part of the world?

definitions.text: hours in this part of the world?

parts.note: a local is one's regular neighbourhood pub; the possessive adds no letters
The Times is a British daily newspaper

explanation.surface: Someone asks when the pub opens each day around here.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pub's daily hours' reads as opening times, but it splits into a pub's name and a newspaper's.
explanation.definitionFit: The time kept in a given region or time zone is that place's clock reading, so these are the hours here.

clue.text: Roof space: length 0-12″

parts.note: the figure zero looks like the letter O
twelve inches make one foot, abbreviated FT

explanation.surface: An attic is measured up: its length runs from nothing to a foot.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads like a measurement range; each symbol stands for letters: L, O, and FT for twelve inches (a foot).
explanation.definitionFit: An attic or storage area directly under a pitched roof is commonly called by this name.

clue.text: Stein in Crete whisked up batter?

indicators.note: whisking ingredients mixes them thoroughly, so the letters of the chef's first name and the island are jumbled together

parts.note: Rick Stein is a well-known British TV chef

explanation.surface: A celebrity chef on holiday in Crete beats up a batter mix.
explanation.walkthrough: Kitchen words mislead: 'batter' is not a pancake mix but a player who bats. Rick Stein is a British TV chef.
explanation.definitionFit: In cricket the player wielding the bat is a batter, one kind of player of the sport.

clue.text: Record playing that can provide a way in

definitions.text: that can provide a way in

parts.note: to log is to record, and a log is a written record
on means playing or performing, as in a show being on

explanation.surface: A record being played acts as a gateway to something.
explanation.definitionFit: Entering credentials to gain access to a computer system is the act that gives a user entry.

clue.text: Fit in untidy heaps

indicators.note: something untidy is disordered, so the letters of heaps are arranged messily

explanation.surface: Things are crammed into messy piles.
explanation.definitionFit: Being physically healthy and in good condition is what fitness means, so the phrase is a synonym.

clue.text: Constant as Douglas's cats?

definitions.meaning: something constant never stops, going on without any finish
Douglas is the capital of the Isle of Man, whose Manx cats famously have no tails

explanation.surface: Someone compares persistence to a particular person's cats.
explanation.walkthrough: Douglas is not a person but the capital of the Isle of Man; Manx cats are born tailless, so their back ends lack a tail.
explanation.definitionFit: Unceasing, perpetual things never stop, a plain synonym for constant; tailless cats lack an end, the joking second sense.

clue.text: Caught with joint in nick

parts.note: C is the cricket scorecard abbreviation for caught
the hip is a joint of the body

explanation.surface: Someone is arrested with cannabis and taken to the police station.
explanation.walkthrough: 'joint' and 'nick' suggest drugs and a police cell (British slang for prison or police station), but nick here means a small notch.
explanation.definitionFit: A small notch or flake broken off a surface is a nick, an everyday synonym.

clue.text: Hang around shack eventually changing hands

indicators.note: eventually points at the final letter, and changing hands swaps left for right, the letters L and R

parts.note: a hovel is a crude, squalid dwelling, much like a shack

explanation.surface: Someone loiters near a hut that is finally being sold.
explanation.walkthrough: 'changing hands' sounds like a sale; it means swapping L (left) for R (right) at the end of the word.
explanation.definitionFit: To linger in one place, hanging in the air or loitering nearby, is a synonym of to remain near.

clue.text: Pressure is on in Herts town to supply engine part

parts.note: P is the physics symbol for pressure

indicators.note: in places the word on inside the name of the town

parts.note: Tring is a small town in Hertfordshire (Herts), England

explanation.surface: Pressure is building in a Hertfordshire town that makes motor components.
explanation.walkthrough: Tring is a market town in Hertfordshire, a county north of London.
explanation.definitionFit: A sealing band fitted around a cylinder's moving plunger is a component in internal combustion engines.

clue.text: Pedant succeeded with puzzle

parts.note: S is the genealogical abbreviation for succeeded
a tickler is a puzzling problem, as in brain-tickler

explanation.surface: A fussy person managed to solve a brain-teaser.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who insists on strict rules and exactness is a fusspot, the same as a nitpicking pedant.

clue.text: Showing contempt for losing out in short-lived affair

indicators.note: losing means the word out is dropped from the longer word

parts.note: flouting a rule is openly showing contempt for it

explanation.surface: Someone scorns being left out of a brief romance.
explanation.definitionFit: A brief, casual romantic or sexual relationship is a common sense of this word.

clue.text: Edna anonymously appearing in Cornish resort to get tranquillisers

indicators.note: appearing in places the shortened name inside the resort's name

parts.note: St Ives is a seaside resort in Cornwall

indicators.note: anonymous means without a name, and N is the abbreviation for name, so N is dropped

explanation.surface: A woman named Edna, incognito in a Cornish seaside town, obtains calming pills.
explanation.walkthrough: St Ives is a seaside town in Cornwall, south-west England; 'anonymously' works because N is the usual abbreviation for name.
explanation.definitionFit: Drugs that calm a person or induce sleep are sedatives, a near synonym of tranquillisers.

clue.text: Shock about family's use of cosmetics etc

indicators.note: about means the word for a fright surrounds the word for relatives

parts.note: a scare is a sudden shock
kin means one's family or relatives

explanation.surface: A family is horrified by how much make-up is being used.
explanation.walkthrough: 'family's' means family has, a link to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Applying creams, lotions and make-up to keep a complexion healthy is the regime this word names.

clue.text: Note Greek ship or what it could carry

parts.note: C is a musical note
the Argo was the ship of Jason and the Argonauts in Greek myth

explanation.surface: Someone records a Greek vessel, or perhaps its load.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition points back at the ship: what it could carry is its freight.
explanation.definitionFit: Goods carried by a ship or aircraft are its freight, which is what a vessel transports.

clue.text: Iron matter turned into cyborg

indicators.note: turned means the letters of the two words are turned into a new order

explanation.surface: Iron metal is transformed into a part-machine being.
explanation.walkthrough: The Terminator is the cyborg killer in the James Cameron films.
explanation.definitionFit: The title character of the Terminator films is a robotic assassin with living tissue, a famous example of a cyborg.

clue.text: Most violent end

definitions.meaning: as an adjective it means the most severe or intense
as a noun it means the furthest point or limit, as in at one end of the scale

explanation.surface: Someone describes the fiercest kind of finish.
explanation.definitionFit: Severe or drastic in the highest degree is one sense, and the outermost limit or edge is the other.

clue.text: Risked cold being replaced by extremes of emotion and brought about an improvement

indicators.note: being replaced by swaps the letter for cold with the edge letters of the next word

parts.note: to chance something is to risk it
C is the abbreviation for cold, as on a tap

indicators.note: extremes are the outer letters, the first and last of the word emotion

explanation.surface: Someone gambled, warmed up emotionally and things got better.
explanation.definitionFit: To enhance is to improve or heighten the quality of something, so the past tense means made better.

clue.text: Magazine welcomed by senior as part of the breakfast ritual?

indicators.note: welcomed by means taken in, so the magazine's name sits inside the abbreviation

parts.note: The Oldie is a British magazine for older readers

explanation.surface: An elderly person reads a magazine as part of the morning routine.
explanation.walkthrough: The Oldie is a British humour and lifestyle magazine. 'Magazine' also misleads toward a gun's magazine, fitting a soldier.
explanation.definitionFit: In Britain a thin strip of toast for dipping into a boiled egg is called a soldier, a breakfast staple.

clue.text: Stylish runny brie scoffed, being drunk

parts.note: in means fashionable or stylish

indicators.note: a runny cheese is losing its shape, so the letters of brie run out of order

parts.note: to scoff food is to eat it greedily, so scoffed gives ate

explanation.surface: A smart guest gobbles ripe runny brie while tipsy.
explanation.definitionFit: As an adjective this formal word describes someone intoxicated, a synonym of drunk.

clue.text: That woman frequents bar where footballers may be found in Hackney

definitions.text: where footballers may be found in Hackney

indicators.note: frequents means is often found in, so the pronoun sits inside the chocolate bar's name

parts.note: a Mars bar is a chocolate bar
she refers to that woman

explanation.surface: A woman regularly visits a pub where football players hang out in east London.
explanation.walkthrough: Hackney Marshes in east London is famous for its dozens of amateur football pitches. Mars is a chocolate bar, not a pub.
explanation.definitionFit: Hackney Marshes is a large open space of Sunday-league pitches, the place local footballers play.

clue.text: Southern chipotle cooked after cutting the end and top of it could make mess

indicators.note: cooking transforms ingredients, so the remaining letters of the chilli are rearranged
after cutting means once the top letter of it has also been removed from the chilli's name
the end of a word is its final letter, here the last letter of chipotle, which is dropped
the top of a word is its first letter

explanation.surface: Cooking a spicy chilli carelessly could leave a stain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'after cutting' removes I (top of 'it') and E (the end of chipotle), leaving CHPOTL; 'cooked' rearranges that into PLOTCH.
explanation.definitionFit: A splotch is a messy spot or smear, a mark that makes a mess on a surface.

clue.text: Poles holding unruly rogue who is handy with a knife

definitions.text: who is handy with a knife

indicators.note: holding means the two pole letters enclose the rearranged word

parts.note: S and N are the south and north poles

indicators.note: unruly means disorderly, so the letters of rogue are disordered

explanation.surface: Polish men restrain a disorderly villain who wields a blade.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Poles' looks like Polish people; it is the south and north poles, S and N.
explanation.definitionFit: A medical doctor who operates uses a scalpel skilfully, so is literally adept with a blade.

clue.text: Former striker, he's rare wanting work

indicators.note: wanting work means needing to be worked on, so the letters are reworked into a new order

parts.note: the letters of he's, without the apostrophe

explanation.surface: An ex-footballer is rarely seen and is looking for a job.
explanation.walkthrough: Alan Shearer is a former England and Newcastle United centre-forward, the Premier League's record scorer.
explanation.definitionFit: Alan Shearer was a famous England centre-forward, so he is an example of an ex-striker in football.

clue.text: News about variable look for material

indicators.note: about means the letters for news go around the other pieces

parts.note: N stands for new, so news is taken as two of them, N and N
Y is a variable in algebra
lo is an old word meaning look

explanation.surface: Reports about how something changeable looks for a fabric.
explanation.definitionFit: A synthetic fibre used to make fabric, stockings and rope is a kind of material.

clue.text: Lighter top going for pound which is generous

indicators.note: the top letter goes, and the letter for a pound takes its place

parts.note: a lighter is a flat-bottomed barge used to unload ships
L is the abbreviation for a pound sterling, from Latin libra

explanation.surface: A cigarette lighter swaps its top for a coin, which is kind.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lighter' is not a flame-maker but a barge.
explanation.definitionFit: A generous helping is a big one, so the word means ample or plentiful.

clue.text: Left on grumpy donkey, abandoning yen for quiet sheltered beach

indicators.note: abandoning means the letter for yen is given up in exchange for the letters for quiet

parts.note: Eeyore is the gloomy donkey in Winnie-the-Pooh
Y is the symbol for the Japanese yen
sh is a call for quiet

explanation.surface: Someone sets off on a sulky donkey, giving up money for peace on a protected beach.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface swaps Y for SH in EEYORE, giving EESHORE.
explanation.definitionFit: The lee is the sheltered side, so this phrase is read as a shore protected from wind.

clue.text: Statement of resignation they hope provides a case

indicators.note: the words they hope form a case around the answer's letters, which sit inside them

explanation.surface: A sigh of acceptance from people who are still hopeful that something will happen.
explanation.definitionFit: A weary exclamation showing that one accepts something disappointing, roughly 'oh well'.

clue.text: Porridge can make you churn

definitions.meaning: porridge is British slang for a prison sentence
to churn is to agitate or mix, as with a spoon

explanation.surface: Making porridge involves churning it in a pan.
explanation.walkthrough: Porridge is British slang for time in prison, as in the sitcom Porridge.
explanation.definitionFit: Slang for jail fits the prison sense, and mixing with a spoon or paddle fits to churn.

clue.text: Cause of misery — troops lurking between hills …

indicators.note: lurking between means the soldiers sit hidden between two hills

parts.note: a tor is a rocky hill, especially on Dartmoor; plural hills gives two of them
men are troops or soldiers

explanation.surface: Soldiers hiding in the hills are the source of suffering.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who torments others makes them suffer, so is a source of their misery.

clue.text: … still suppressing a small source of uprising

indicators.note: suppressing means holding down inside, so the word for still encloses the other letters

parts.note: yet means still, as in 'yet to come'

explanation.surface: The clue continues: troops are still crushing a minor revolt.
explanation.walkthrough: 'uprising' suggests rebellion; it is dough rising in baking.
explanation.definitionFit: Bread dough rises because the fungus used in baking produces gas, the cause of its swelling.

clue.text: One's got out of bed to go on the roof

definitions.meaning: a tall marsh grass grows in a ... bed, so one is taken out of such a bed
dried stems of this marsh plant are used for thatching roofs

explanation.surface: Someone got up and climbed onto the roof.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bed' is not a sleeping place but a reed bed, a patch of marsh where these plants grow.
explanation.definitionFit: Thatched roofs are made from bundles of dried stems from water plants grown in marsh beds.

clue.text: Classic vehicle driver, fancy hot racer touring Italy and then Europe

indicators.note: fancy means elaborate or imaginative, so the whole collection of letters is fancifully rearranged
touring means travelling about, so the letters of hot racer roam around those for Italy and Europe and the whole set ends up mixed

parts.note: I is the international vehicle code for Italy

explanation.surface: A souped-up sports car tours Italy and moves on to the rest of Europe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Classic' means classical antiquity, not a vintage car. 'fancy' and 'touring' mix HOT RACER with I and E; the two single letters land in separate gaps, so this is one pooled rearrangement.
explanation.definitionFit: A charioteer drove a chariot, the horse-drawn vehicle of classical Greece and Rome.
